metadata.title: How Does Claude Rank AI-Readiness Across a Portfolio?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude decides, using its own judgment, which portfolio company is most ready for AI investment -- or is doing something narrower. Lands the carry-out that a ranked AI-readiness list is a ranking built from what this quarter's updates actually say, waiting for an operating partner's call, not Claude's judgment about which company is smartest to back.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carries real skill-specific facts (not unfilled template placeholders) -- see QUESTION.md. Facts preserved: the ai-readiness skill scans the portfolio for the highest-leverage AI opportunities and ranks where to deploy operating-partner time; it ingests quarterly updates and financials across portfolio companies, identifies quick wins at each, and stacks them into one ranked action list; used during quarterly portfolio reviews, annual planning, or when deciding which companies get AI investment first. Register re-registered Teardown -> Plain; source's B03 design-tell verdict became a plain mechanism + both-directions beat; a wrong-guess beat and an anchor (one portfolio company's Q3 update: ingested -> quick wins found -> scored -> ranked -> stopped, waiting) were added per hai-simple's Phase 1 structure, since the source's Teardown shape carried neither.

beats.narration_text: Someone asks whether Claude decides, using its own judgment, which portfolio company is most ready for AI. It doesn't — and once you see the wiring, you'll see why. Liam, in for Bear.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What decides which portco -- judgment?', hesitates on 'judgment', corrects to 'the update', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('judgment' -> 'the update') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: The intuitive read is that Claude weighs the whole portfolio and picks the smartest bet — a judgment call. That's not what's happening. What the skill actually does, per company, is ingest the quarterly update and the financials, then extract the AI quick wins the update already names. Feed it a company whose update never mentions AI, and it won't invent one. Nothing in the source text, nothing gets ranked for that company this quarter. That's the first design choice worth naming: they optimized for being grounded in the operator's own words, at the cost of catching opportunities the operator forgot to write down.

shot.new_visual_element: A judgment figure weighing which portco is 'most ready', struck through; a written ingest/identify/rank procedure lit instead

production_viz.label: Judgment, struck -- ingest/identify/rank, lit
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a figure icon labelled 'JUDGMENT' beside a thought-bubble of scattered decision marks. Right: a numbered card labelled 'INGEST / IDENTIFY / RANK'. The judgment side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the procedure side stays lit. A final line reads 'no mention in update -- nothing ranked' and the figure does not reach for it.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening, mechanically. For each portfolio company, the skill ingests the quarterly update and the financials, extracts the quick wins written in the text, and stacks them into a single ranked action list. Nothing more. Watch one company travel through the pipeline — Portco A, Q3 update. Ingested. Quick wins identified. Scored against the spec's criteria. Placed in the ranked stack. Then the pipeline halts. It doesn't decide, recommend, or approve. It hands you a sorted list and stops.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- one portfolio company's Q3 update traveling ingested -> quick wins found -> scored -> ranked, then stopping

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one portco, four stops
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four stacked cards labelled 'INGESTED', 'QUICK WINS FOUND', 'SCORED', 'RANKED'. A single highlighted token 'PORTCO A · Q3 UPDATE' travels down through all four cards in turn, each lighting as it arrives. At the bottom, the token halts beside a label 'in the stack, waiting' -- it does not continue past the ranked card. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, PAID OFF, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The ranking is built — ingested, scored, placed in the stack, ready for review. Now read it honestly in both directions. A high rank means the update scored well against the spec's criteria; it does not mean this is the single best next AI investment across the whole portfolio. And a company that ranks low this quarter doesn't mean there's no AI opportunity there — it can just mean this update didn't mention one, which sits outside what the skill can see. That's the trade-off in the design: they optimized for a defensible, text-grounded ranking at the expense of any judgment that would look past what's written. Either way, the list waits for an operating partner's call before anything gets funded.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS, ranked and waiting; splits into 'scored well is not best overall' and 'ranked low is not no opportunity'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- ranked, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 FOUR-CARD COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical placement, the token resting at the 'RANKED' card beside 'in the stack, waiting'. It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'SCORED: WELL' with a checkmark, then a struck-through 'BEST OVERALL?' beneath it, labelled 'scored well is not best overall'; right reads 'RANKED LOW' beside a faint 'no mention this quarter' note, labelled 'ranked low is not no opportunity'.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Give Claude one portfolio company's latest quarterly update and financials, and ask it to run the ai-readiness skill: identify the quick wins, rank where AI investment should go first. Then hand it a company update that never mentions AI at all and run the same skill again — watch what the skill does when there's nothing in the source text to work from. That's the design choice, live. Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Give me one portfolio company's latest quarterly update and financials. Run the ai-readiness skill: identify the quick wins, rank where AI investment should go first. Then hand it a company update that never mentions AI at all and try the same skill again.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no CLI required. Play the role of the ai-readiness skill. Given one portfolio company's quarterly update, extract every AI quick win the text actually mentions, quoting the specific line for each. Score each on effort, time-to-value, and dollar impact. Rank them into one action list. Then say plainly which quick wins you did not invent, because they weren't in the source. Go deeper: what would you change about that ranking if you also had the CEO's private notes and last quarter's board deck — and where would that pull the design away from being defensible?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how an AI-readiness skill turns a portfolio company's quarterly update into a ranked action list. Below I'll paste a real (or realistic) quarterly update for one company. Play the role of that skill and do four things: (1) extract every AI-relevant quick win the update actually mentions, quoting the specific sentence or bullet for each; (2) score each on effort (S/M/L), time-to-value (weeks/quarters), and dollar impact (rough range); (3) rank them into a single stacked action list; and (4) tell me plainly which plausible AI quick wins you did NOT invent, because they were not in the text. Be honest about what the source did and didn't say. [Paste the quarterly update below.]
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what would you change about that ranking if you also had the CEO's private notes and last quarter's board deck — and where would that pull the design away from being defensible in a partner meeting?
